newsitem.title: UK: British Airways ground staff back strike.
newsitem.headline: British Airways ground staff back strike.

text.p: A second group of workers at British Airways Plc voted for strike action on Monday as ground staff voted to strike in protest against the airline's decision to sell off its catering unit.

The ground staff's verdict follows last week's ballot decision by cabin crew which overwhelmingly voted for industrial action in a bitter five-month row over pay and conditions and increased the likelihood disruption to flights.

The Transport and General Workers Union (T&G) said 9,508 workers, representing 90 percent of BA's ground staff were balloted, out of which 69 percent had returned their votes. It said 62.5 percent of them had voted in favour of the strike.
T&G's national secretary for aviation, George Ryde, told reporters there would be a meeting later on Monday with BA's cabin crew staff to discuss whether they would go ahead with a strike.
A similar meeting with the ground staff was scheduled for Tuesday morning, with a final decision expected later this week.

Commenting on the ground staff ballot, Ryde said, "The mood among members is confident and we are amazed by the result given the level of intimidation of BA.". He called on the airline to respond and said he was willing to attend arbitration talks to resolve the disputes.
BA has unveiled strong tactics in recent days to break the strike mood. It told staff over the weekend strikers could be sacked and sued for damages.
Responding to BA's stand, Ryder accused the airline of terrorising its workers saying: "I don't believe BA ever bluffs but nor do we".
News of the verdict further hit BA shares, which were down 10 1/2 pence at 685p as analysts warned the cost of confrontation would be heavy if passengers defected.
The two ballots stem from different issues but are both linked to BA's cost-cutting moves to save one billion pounds ($1.7 billion) by 2000.
Analysts said the impact on BA profits could be heavy, especially if passengers decided to start switching airlines.
"A strike would make a massive difference to BA -- financially in the short term as well as hurting it long-term," said Chris Avery, analyst at Paribas.
Avery warned that BA's lucrative business traveller community would not be likely to take on a strike risk.

"As a businessman, if there's a risk that you won't get to a meeting in Tokyo or New York in two weeks' time due to the threat of disruption, you will book with someone else now. Not wait until tomorrow."
"What you have to consider is people who switch away may find it's not so bad elsewhere and BA then faces the task of having to win customers back."
Industry observers pointed out that when BA faced the threat of a pilots' strike last year, which failed to materialise, the cost to profits was far from negligible.
"That dispute cost them more than 10 million pounds," said another transport analyst, even though no action took place.

BA has drawn up a battle-plan to keep services flying. All management have been re-trained to allow them to take on more roles, extra security will be brought in to get strike breakers through picket-lines and the group is also willing to hire external staff to take on BA strikers' jobs.
"BA is staking a lot on this," said one travel industry insider. "It's investing a lot of money and ruling by fear. Not very nice. But I guess that's commerce."

The airline, fresh from a 60 million pounds facelift and in the midst of seeking regulatory clearance for its alliance with AMR's American Airlines, has placed all operations on red alert to combat the threat.
Chief Executive Robert Ayling cancelled his planned trip to witness the handover of Hong Kong in order to take on British unions instead.
"The big issue for BA is control of its cost base," summed up one transport analyst. "BA needs to win this one and end the showdown with the unions for good." ($ = 0.601 British Pounds)
